# Welcome {.unnumbered}

This book documents the Rust port of Mark Hill's original FRESCALO Fortran
suite (`sampdist_1.f`, `neighsim_1.f`, `Frescalo_1.f`), one chapter per Rust
function.

Each chapter's code cell is the **authoritative source** for that function:
editing the code block in a chapter and re-rendering the book (or running
`python3 tools/tangle.py` directly) writes the updated code into the correct
location in the corresponding file under `../src/`, replacing only the
region between its `// @tangle:start <id>` / `// @tangle:end <id>` markers.
Everything else in the `.rs` files — imports, struct/impl scaffolding,
surrounding functions — is left untouched.

The book is organized by source file, in the order the pipeline runs:
`src/lib.rs` (shared support code used by all three binaries), then
`sampdist`, `neighsim`, and `frescalo`.

See `../README.md` for the fidelity audit against the original Fortran and
the list of intentionally preserved quirks/bugs.

## The method, and how to read the "What this does" boxes

Alongside the code, most chapters carry a short **"What this does"** section
aimed at ecologists rather than programmers: what the function means for
your occurrence data, not how it's implemented. Where a function
corresponds to a specific step of the FRESCALO method, that section links
it back to the relevant part of the paper the method comes from:

> Hill, M.O. (2012) Local frequency as a key to interpreting species
> occurrence data when recording effort is not known. *Methods in Ecology
> and Evolution*, 3, 195–205.
> [doi:10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00146.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2011.00146.x)

A copy is also kept at `../Original_frescalo/`. Many functions in
`src/lib.rs`, however, are plumbing (fixed-width text parsing, sorting,
console output, Fortran-style number formatting) that the paper never
discusses directly — those chapters say so plainly rather than forcing a
connection that isn't there.
